blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text: Definition:-Compounds having similar molecular and structural formula but differing in the stereo chemical formula and behaviour towards plane polarised light are called optical isomers and this phenomenon is called optical isomerism.

blocks.title: Condition for optical activity
blocks.text: The molecule should be asymmetric or chiral i.e. symmetry element (POS & COS) should be absent.

blocks.title: Chiral carbon
blocks.text: The carbon atom linked to four different groups is called chiral carbon

blocks.title: Representation of molecules
blocks.text:
Fischer projection: An optical isomer can be represented by Fischer projection which is planar representation of three dimensional structure.

Wedge-dash notation is a method used to represent the three-dimensional structure of molecules on a two-dimensional surface. It helps visualize the spatial arrangement of atoms and bonds in a molecule.

blocks.title: Example-01
blocks.question:
Q.1.A chiral carbon atom is one that?

a) Is bonded to four different groups

b) Is bonded to two identical groups

c) Is bonded to three different groups

d) Is bonded to two different groups
blocks.answer:
Ans-(a) Is bonded to four different groups

Explanation:

A chiral carbon atom (also called an asymmetric carbon) four different groups or atoms. This arrangement makes the carbon atom the centre of asymmetry and allows for the existence of stereoisomers or enantiomers).

blocks.title: Example-02
blocks.question:
Q.2. How many chiral centers are present in 2-chlorobutane?

a) 0

b) 1

c) 2

d) 3
blocks.answer:
Answer: (b) 1

Explanation:

In 2-chlorobutane, the second carbon is bonded to four different groups:

  • A methyl group (-CH₃)
  • An ethyl group (-CH₂CH₃)
  • A chlorine atom (-Cl)
  • A hydrogen atom (-H)
This makes it a chiral centre, while the other carbons do not have four different groups attached. Hence, there is 1 chiral center.

blocks.title: Example-03
blocks.question:
Q.3.How many chiral carbon atoms are there in glucose?

a) 0

b)1

c) 2

d) 4
blocks.answer:
Answer: (d) 4

Explanation:

The structure of glucose (in its open-chain form) contains six carbon atoms. Out of these, four carbons (C-2, C-3, C-4, and C-5) are chiral centers because they are bonded to four different groups.

Thus, glucose has 4 chiral carbon atoms.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text: Configuration refers to the spatial arrangement of atoms or groups in a molecule. In the context of optical isomerism, it specifically relates to the three-dimensional arrangement of groups around a chiral center.

blocks.title: Configuration of optical isomer
blocks.text:
• Absolute configuration (R/S system)
    • Relative configuration (D/L system)

blocks.title: Determination of R/S configuration
blocks.text:
Rule-1Assign the priority to the four groups attached to the chiral carbon according to priority rule.

Rule-2 If lowest priority  is bonded to vertical line then moving 1-2-3

Rule-3 If lowest priority  is bonded to horizontal line then moving 3-2-1

blocks.title: CIP SEQUENCE RULE
blocks.text:
The following rules are followed for deciding the precedence order of the atoms or groups :-

• Highest priority is assigned to the atoms of higher atomic number attached to asymmetric carbon atom.
    • In case of isotopes, isotopes having higher atomic mass is given priority.
    • If the first atom of a group attached to asymmetric carbon atom is same then we consider the atomic number of 2nd atom or subsequent atoms in group.
    • If there is a double bond or triple bond, both atoms are considered to be duplicated or triplicated.

blocks.title: DETERMINATION OF D/L SYSTEM
blocks.text:
• Reference molecule glyceraldehyde
    • It is used to assign configuration in carbohydrate, amino acid and similar compounds

Rule: Arrange parent carbon chain on the vertical line

• Placed most oxidised carbon on the top or nearest to top.
    • On highest IUPAC numbered chiral carbon

If OH group on RHS = D

If OH group on LHS = L

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
Question 1

What is the absolute configuration of the 2-butanol molecule shown below?

A) R

B) S

C) E

D) Z
blocks.answer:
Answer: A) R

Explanation:

Prioritize Groups: Assign priority based on atomic number: -OH (1), -CH₂CH₃ (2), -CH₃ (3), -H (4).

Orient Molecule: The lowest priority group (-H) is pointing away (dash).

Trace Path: The path from priority 1 → 2 → 3 is clockwise.

So, The Configuration is R

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
The stereoisomer which shows different behavior towards plane polarized light are known as optical isomer.

Dextrorotatory: A compound is dextrorotatory if it rotates plane-polarized light in a clockwise direction. It is often denoted by the symbol (+) or (d).

Levorotatory: A compound is levorotatory if it rotates plane-polarized light in a counterclockwise direction. It is often denoted by the symbol (-) or (l).

blocks.title: Enantiomers
blocks.text: Non-superimposable mirror images are called enantiomers which rotate the plane polarised light up to same extent but in opposite direction.

blocks.title: Diastereomers
blocks.text: stereoisomers which are not mirror images of each other. They have different physical and chemical properties.

blocks.title: Meso compounds
blocks.text: Those compounds whose molecules are superimposable on their mirror images inspite of the presence of asymmetric carbon atom.

blocks.title: Racemic mixture
blocks.text:
An equimolar mixture of the enantiomers (d & l) is called racemic mixture. The process of converting d- or l) form of an optically active compound into racemic form is called racemisation.

It does not rotate plane-polarized light because the rotations of the enantiomers cancel each other out.

blocks.title: Resolution
blocks.text: The process by which d l mixture is separated into d and l forms with the help of chiral reagents or chiral catalyst is known as resolution.

blocks.title: Some Important Points
blocks.text:
Compound containing chiral carbon may or may not be optically active but show optical isomerism.

For optical isomer chiral carbon is not the necessary condition.

blocks.title: Example -1
blocks.question:
The specific rotation of a racemic mixture is:

(a) Positive

(b) Negative

(c) Zero

(d) Variable
blocks.answer:
Answer: (c) Zero

Explanation:

A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of two enantiomers (optical isomers) that rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions with equal magnitude but opposite signs. As a result, their effects cancel each other out, and the net-specific rotation is zero.

modules.name: Calculation of the number of optical isomers

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
The key to calculating the number of optical isomers in a molecule is to identify the

chiral centers. A chiral center is a carbon atom bonded to four different groups.

blocks.title: Formula for Calculating Optical Isomers
blocks.text:
For unsymmetrical molecules

  • Number of optical isomers = $2^n$
  • Where "n" is the number of chiral centers in the molecule
For symmetrical molecules:-

  • If 'n' is even (here n is the number of chiral centres):      • Number of optically  active = $2^{n-1}$
      • Number of meso compounds = $2^{n/2-1}$
      • Total number of optical isomers = $2^{n-1} + 2^{n/2-1}$
  • If 'n' is odd:      • Number of optically  active  = $2^{n-1} - 2^{(n-1)/2}$
      • Number of meso compounds = $2^{(n-1)/2}$
  • • Total number of optical isomers = $2^{n-1}$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
How many total optically active isomers are possible for following structure?

(a)6

(b)8

(c)4

(d)9
blocks.answer:
Ans-(b) 8.

The maximum number of possible stereoisomers for a molecule with n chiral centers is given by the formula 2ⁿ.

In this case, n = 3 (three chiral centers). So, the maximum number of possible stereoisomers is 2³= 8.

Therefore, the answer is (b) 8.

In this case, n = 3 (three stereo centers). So, the maximum number of possible stereoisomers is 2³ = 8.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: Structural isomerism occurs when compounds have the same molecular formula but different connectivity of atoms, resulting in distinct structures and properties.

blocks.title: Key Points: Types of Structural Isomers
blocks.text:
Chain Isomerism(C.I.)

  • Definition: Isomers differ in the carbon chain (straight vs. branched).
  • Example:
Position Isomerism (P.I.)

  • Definition: Isomers differ in the position of a functional group, substituent, or double/triple bond.
  • Example
Functional Group Isomerism(F.G.I.)

  • Definition: Compounds which have the same molecular formula but different functional groups are functional group isomers.
  • Example:
Metamerism

  • Definition: Compounds which have the same molecular formula, and the same functional group but different alkyl groups attached to a polyvalent functional group
  • Example

blocks.title: Degree of Unsaturation / Double Bond Equivalent/ Index of Hydrogen Deficiency
blocks.text:
D.U/D.B.E./I.H.D. = No. of π bond + No. of rings

If D.U. = 0 (Νο π bond/ring)

D.U. = 1 (1 π bond/1 ring)

D.U. = 2 (2 π bonds/2 rings/1 π bond + 1 ring/1 triple bond)

blocks.title: Number of Structural Isomers
blocks.text:
The number of structural isomers possible for $C_4H_{10}O$  is 7.

$C_4H_{10}O$  D.U= 0 (no π bond), so only alcohols and ethers are formed.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
Consider the given set of compounds: pentane, butane, 2-methyl butane, and propane. The number of pairs of isomers possible will be_____.

A. 1
B. 2
C. 4
D. 3
blocks.answer:
Answer: A

Solution: Chemical compounds with identical formulas but different physical or chemical properties are named isomers. Therefore, only pentane and 2-methyl butane can show isomerism because they have the same chemical formula $C_5H_{12}$ and the number of possible pairs is equal to 1.

So, option A is the correct answer.

blocks.title: Geometrical isomerism (G.I.)
blocks.text:
Geometrical isomerism (G.I.): Different configuration due to restricted rotation.

• Alkenes (>C=C<), oximes (>C=N—) and azo compounds [—N=N—] etc.,   show G.I. due to restricted rotation about double bond.

• Cycloalkanes show G.I. due to restricted rotation about single bond in ring.

Condition for Geometrical Isomerism

• Only those alkenes show G. I. in which "Each
$\mathrm{sp}^2$ carbon have different atoms or groups"

• In cycloalkane system; atleast two
$\mathbf{s p}^3$ hybrid atom of ring individually must have different atoms / groups attached to it.

Nomenclature systems of geometrical isomers with configuration

Cis-Trans configuration

If same groups are at same side then cis and if same groups are at different side then trans.

blocks.text:
• Dipole moment :

Example: But-2-ene

Therefore, cis > trans (Dipole moment).

• Polarity α μ (Dipole moment)

Generally, cis > trans

• Boiling Point (B.P.):

Generally, cis molecule has higher boiling point than trans molecule due to more polarity.

• Melting point:

Melting point depends on packing efficiency.

blocks.title: Calculation of total number of geometrical isomerism
blocks.text:
When compound is unsymmetrical No. of G.I. = $2^{\mathrm{n}}$

When compound is symmetrical No. of G.I. =  $2^{\mathrm{n}-1}+2^{\mathrm{p}-1}$

where  $\mathrm{p}=\frac{\mathrm{n}}{2}$ (when n is  even) and $\mathrm{p}=\frac{\mathrm{n}+1}{2}$ (when n is odd)

where n = no. of restricted rotatory system (double bond) about which G.I. is possible

blocks.title: Conformational isomerism / Rotational isomerism / Conformations
blocks.text:
• The different arrangement of atoms in space that result from the rotation around single bond are called conformations. The phenomenon is called conformational isomerism.
  • Bond length, bond angle are same in all the conformers.
  • These are interconvertible forms of a same compound so there is no change in boiling point, melting point, dipole moment.
  • There are infinite conformations of a compound
  • If there are three continuous single bond present in a compound then it shows conformation.
Conformations of ethane $\left[\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_3\right]$:

In ethane, staggered form is more stable than eclipsed form by 12.5 kJ/mol.

blocks.title: Some Important Terms
blocks.text:
• Dihedral Angle/ Torsional Angle : The angle between two bonds of adjacent atoms.
Dihedral Angle: The dihedral angle in the eclipsed form of ethane is 0°and  in the staggered form is 60°.

  • Types of strain
Conformations of butane:

$\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_3$

I (Fully eclipsed form): In this form distance between two methyl groups is minimum so maximum

repulsion or minimum stable. IV (Anti or staggered): In this form distance between two methyl groups is maximum so minimum

repulsion or maximum stability.

III (Gauche form): In this form, the angle between two methyl groups is 60°

Stability order: IV > II > III > I

Energy order: I > III > II > IV

Note: If staggered form is at 60° (in ethane) then it is not gauche form.

Special Cases:

It is not necessary that anti-conformation is always more stable than gauche conformation.

• Dihedral Angle/ Torsional Angle : The angle between two bonds of adjacent atoms.
Dihedral Angle: The dihedral angle in the eclipsed form of ethane is 0°and  in the staggered form is 60°.

  • Types of strain
Conformations of butane:

$\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_3$

I (Fully eclipsed form): In this form distance between two methyl groups is minimum so maximum

repulsion or minimum stable. IV (Anti or staggered): In this form distance between two methyl groups is maximum so minimum

repulsion or maximum stability.

III (Gauche form): In this form, the angle between two methyl groups is 60°

Stability order: IV > II > III > I

Energy order: I > III > II > IV

Note: If staggered form is at 60° (in ethane) then it is not gauche form.

Special Cases:

It is not necessary that anti-conformation is always more stable than gauche conformation.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing functional group isomers with chain or position isomers.
  • Missing possible isomers due to incomplete visualization of structures.
  • Ignoring IUPAC naming rules for correct identification.
  • Overlooking stereoisomerism differences.

blocks.title: Calculation of total number of geometrical isomerism
blocks.text:
When compound is unsymmetrical No. of G.I. = $2^{\mathrm{n}}$

When compound is symmetrical No. of G.I. =  $2^{\mathrm{n}-1}+2^{\mathrm{p}-1}$

where  $\mathrm{p}=\frac{\mathrm{n}}{2}$ (when n is  even) and $\mathrm{p}=\frac{\mathrm{n}+1}{2}$ (when n is odd)

where n = no. of restricted rotatory system (double bond) about which G.I. is possible
